analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare and boosts federal Medicaid funding for those services.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since June 12, 2025, backed by 5 Democratic senators and no Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add three benefits Medicare does not cover today: dental care (cleanings, fillings, root canals, emergency care, and dentures), vision care (yearly eye exams, eyeglasses, contacts, and low-vision devices), and hearing care (exams and hearing aids). It would also raise the federal Medicaid match to 90% for these services for adults, making it cheaper for states to cover them. Dentists, audiologists, and eye doctors would become paid Medicare providers, and seniors would no longer pay fully out of pocket for dentures, glasses, and hearing aids.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — roughly 67 million older and disabled Americans — who today pay out of pocket for most dental, vision, and hearing care, including the roughly one in five who have no natural teeth. Adult Medicaid enrollees in states that take up the richer 90% federal match would gain coverage of services many states now skip. Dentists, audiologists, optometrists, hearing aid makers, and eyewear sellers gain a large new stream of federally paid patients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and low-income adults needing dental, vision, hearing care

how_it_helps.text: Adds dental coverage to Medicare: two cleanings and two exams per year, fillings, crowns, root canals, extractions, emergency dental care, and dentures (one full upper and lower set every five years).
Adds vision coverage: one routine eye exam per year, eyeglass lenses annually, frames every two years, contact lenses up to $200 per two years, and low-vision devices.
Adds hearing coverage: routine hearing exams, exams for hearing aids, and one hearing aid per ear every four years — services and devices Medicare currently excludes.

Raises the federal Medicaid matching rate to 90% for dental, vision, and hearing services for adults, so states pay only 10 cents of each dollar and have a strong incentive to cover benefits many now skip for adults.
Repeals the statutory grounds on which Medicare excludes routine dental, eyeglasses, eye exams, and hearing aids, so the exclusions cannot simply be reinstated by regulation.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Medicare trust funds and the federal share of Medicaid; the bill contains no dedicated financing or revenue offset, so the cost would add to deficits or have to be found elsewhere. After the phase-in, beneficiaries would still owe the roughly 20% share Medicare does not pay (Medicare pays 80% of the approved amount once fully phased in), plus premiums as usual.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; Medicare beneficiaries owe 20% coinsurance

drawbacks.text: The phase-in is punishing: Medicare would pay providers 0% of the payment amount in the first year and only 10% in the second, ramping to 80% by year eight — meaning in early years the benefit exists on paper but Medicare pays almost nothing, leaving beneficiaries with nearly the full bill until the ramp completes.

The bill has no financing: it creates permanent mandatory spending for a large new Medicare benefit and a richer Medicaid match without any revenue source or offset, which is the main reason proposals like this face trouble in the Finance Committee and score as a large deficit increase.

It gives the Health Secretary sweeping authority to limit or effectively reshape the benefit — prior authorization, minimum hearing-loss thresholds, and authority to modify coverage to match preventive-services recommendations — so the promised benefit is not guaranteed in practice.

Coverage for eyeglasses, contacts, and hearing aids is capped tightly (one pair of lenses per year, frames every two years, $200 in contacts per two years, one hearing aid per ear every four years), which is less generous than the private plans many beneficiaries already buy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and the need is well documented: Medicare has excluded routine dental, eyeglasses, and hearing aids since 1965, and these are precisely the services older and low-income people most often skip because they cost hundreds to thousands of dollars out of pocket. The honest case against is design, not merit: the first years of the phase-in deliver almost no actual payment while building expectations, there is no way to pay for it, and the caps and secretarial discretion leave a thinner benefit than the title promises. A smaller, financed version would have been far easier to defend and pass.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 12, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which controls Medicare and Medicaid legislation — and it has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks introduced the bill on June 12, 2025, with four Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Blumenthal, Fetterman, Merkley, and Welch.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid; the public action history shows nothing after that referral.
No Republican has cosponsored the bill, and the Finance Committee has not scheduled it for consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained from the outcome so far: the bill simply sits in committee, and seniors and Medicaid enrollees continue paying out of pocket for dental, vision, and hearing care. Dental practices, hearing aid makers, and eyewear sellers remain outside Medicare's payment system, and the federal budget is spared new spending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the status quo persists

for.name: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor; it is her first term in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 12, 2025 and has taken no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the public action history.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator has cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred; support so far is entirely Democratic — the sponsor and 4 of 45 Senate Democrats — with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: Dental care would become a Medicare-covered service with a defined payment rate, opening a large new federal revenue stream; today Medicare pays dentists nothing for routine care. Their gain here is the mechanism by which seniors get covered care, so the interests run together.

Medicare would pay for hearing aids (one per ear every four years) and the audiology exams around them, converting one of the most common out-of-pocket purchases for seniors into an insurance-covered one.
Routine eye exams, lenses, frames, and contacts would become payable, and eyewear would be reclassified as durable medical equipment — new covered volume for eye doctors and optical sellers.

Many MA plans market dental, vision, and hearing extras as their main selling point; a universal government benefit for all beneficiaries, including those in traditional Medicare, erodes that advantage even as it raises the value of being a Medicare contractor.
The bill adds permanent new Medicare benefits and a 90% federal Medicaid match with no financing provision, so the cost falls on the Treasury and future taxpayers rather than being offset.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no Republican support, no financing mechanism, and has not been scheduled in the Finance Committee more than seven months after referral. Dental, vision, and hearing benefits have repeatedly appeared in larger Democratic packages (such as Build Back Better) and been dropped for cost; standalone, this bill is very likely to die in committee at the end of the 119th Congress unless it is folded into a broader health or budget package.
